title: Right livelihood
hook: the Buddha names trades to avoid, such as dealing in weapons and poisons (Anguttara Nikaya 5.177)
carry: harm into the hands of someone else

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ihsan: work done with excellence, as though seen. Your line was excellence. Yesterday asked how the work is done; today asks what the work does.

Weapons. Living beings. Meat. Intoxicants. Poison. That's the whole list, and it's short. In a discourse kept in the Anguttara Nikaya, one of the collections of the Buddha's teachings, he names five kinds of trade a lay follower should not take up. He names what changes hands: a sword, a living being sold, a jar of something that clouds the mind, a vial of something that kills. It's a list about what your work puts into the world. Today's word is the step of the Buddhist path it belongs to.
screen: `FIVE TRADES, ONE SHORT LIST.` → `WHAT CHANGES HANDS.` → `WHAT YOUR WORK PUTS OUT.`

segments.voice: First, where it sits. In the teaching Buddhists call the turning of the wheel of the Dhamma, the Buddha lays out the noble eightfold path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. Right livelihood comes just after speech and action. So how you earn is part of the path, the same as how you speak. Second, the list itself. In the Anguttara, the five trades are dealing in weapons, in living beings, in meat, in intoxicants and in poison. The thread through them: each, in its own way, puts harm into the hands of someone else. Third, who it's for. The Buddha speaks these words to his monks, but the rule is about lay followers, people with households and bills. It doesn't tell them to stop working, only which work to leave alone. Buddhist teachers differ on how far to take it today. Some keep closely to the list. Others treat it as a direction more than a fence, and ask of any job: who does this hurt, and could it hurt less? Fourth, why this is harder than it sounds. The list can seem far from an office or a kitchen, but the question underneath goes everywhere. A sales target that pushes someone into a loan they can't carry. Food that's cheap because someone, somewhere, is paid too little. The list is short. The question it leaves behind is not.
screen: `A STEP ON THE EIGHTFOLD PATH.` · `WEAPONS, BEINGS, MEAT, DRINK, POISON.` · `A RULE FOR PEOPLE WITH JOBS.` · `WHO DOES THIS HURT?` · then, large: `RIGHT LIVELIHOOD.`

segments.voice: Let one piece of your work come to mind, a product you sell, a meal you cook, and turn it slowly, like a cup in your hands. Ask the discourse's question of it: does anything harmful change hands here? Often the answer may be no; if something does come up, let it sit beside the breath, and ask what one change would make it a little less harmful, in your own tradition's words if you pray.
Right livelihood. A step on the Buddha's eightfold path: earning a living in a way that does not deal in harm. Today's word.
Your line: harm into the hands of someone else. How you earn is part of the path. That's day eight hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Buddhists list right livelihood as one step of the noble eightfold path, and Buddhist teachers often raise it when lay followers ask how to choose or carry out their work.

chat.says: Does Buddhism say anything about what job you have?
options: Yes: right livelihood, a step on the eightfold path, means earning without dealing in harm.
No, the Buddha's path is for monks; jobs belong to ordinary life, outside of it.
Yes: lay followers are told to quit their jobs so they can meditate full time.
chat.meaning: Right livelihood sits on the eightfold path after speech and action, and the Buddha names trades, like weapons and poison, to leave alone.

Anguttara Nikaya.meaning: one of the collections of the Buddha's teachings

eightfold path.meaning: the Buddha's eight steps, from right view to right concentration

notes: The five trades of AN 5.177 are paraphrased (weapons, living beings, meat, intoxicants, poison); 'living beings' is often explained as human trafficking/slaves. Confirm wording.
The eightfold path is listed in order from SN 56.11; the original-game note calls right livelihood 'the fifth step' per that order. Confirm.
Pali 'samma ajiva' given in Devanagari as सम्मा आजीव; a Buddhist Keeper should confirm the spelling and the pronunciation guide.
'Buddhist teachers differ on how far to take it today' is an attribution without names or counts; confirm phrasing.
SN 56.11 is described only as what Buddhists call the turning of the wheel of the Dhamma; no 'first sermon' claim is made.
